title: What should you ask first in a growth strategy case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a growth strategy case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first how much growth the client wants, by when, and where today's revenue comes from, so you can turn a vague ambition into a gap with a number on it. The trap is answering with a long list of ideas that has no sizes and no order of priority.
body:
The first question to ask

How much growth, by when, and where does today's revenue come from?

"Grow" means nothing until it is a number. "From $50M to $60M in two years" tells you the gap is $10M and that slow bets, like a new product that takes four years to mature, will not close it in time. The revenue split by business unit, product or region tells you where the client is strong and where there is room. Ask, too, whether the goal is revenue or profit: they lead to different answers.

How to build your structure

  • Organic: sell more to current customers, reach new segments or regions, open new channels, launch new products.
  • Inorganic: acquisitions and partnerships.
  • Choose: size each option, then rank by value, speed and risk.

The third bullet is the one most candidates skip, and it is where the marks are. The full tree is in the growth strategy framework.

Turn a growth target into a gap to fill

A gym business has $50M of annual revenue and wants $60M within two years. The $10M gap is 20% growth on today's base. Rather than listing ideas, put a rough size on each lever:

LeverAssumptionRevenue added
New clubs5 clubs at $1M each when mature$5M
Price rise5% on $40M of membership revenueup to $2M
Personal trainingPackages sold to existing members$3M
Total$10M

On paper the gap is closed. Now test each line. New clubs need capital and take time to fill, so $1M each within two years may be optimistic. The price rise is "up to" $2M because some members will cancel: if 3% of them leave, the client loses about $1.26M ($40M × 3% × 1.05), and the rise adds only about $0.74M. It breaks even on revenue if just under 5% leave. Personal training needs qualified trainers the client may not have.

Then look at profit and cash, not only revenue. The price rise costs almost nothing to deliver; new clubs cost a lot up front. A credible answer says where the $10M comes from and what must be true for it to arrive.

The trap most people fall into

A brainstorm with no sizing or priority. Ten ideas of unknown size are worth less than three sized ones with a clear first move. (For generating options quickly, see how to brainstorm with structure.)

Weak: "They could open new clubs, raise prices, add classes, launch an app, sell merchandise, or partner with employers."
Strong: "Three levers could close the $10M gap. Personal training is the fastest and cheapest to test, so I'd start there, then new clubs for the bulk of the growth. I'd hold the price rise until we know how sensitive members are to it."

Two prompts to try

How can a mobile operator increase revenue per customer?

Show the answer
  • Price: plan prices, inflation-linked rises; fewer discounts at renewal.
  • Upgrade: bigger data plans, 5G; handset financing.
  • Add services: insurance, streaming bundles, home broadband, family plans.
  • Keep value: churn of high-value customers; customers moving down to cheaper plans.

Where to start: upgrades and add-on services. Price rises are fastest but risk churn.

The trap: raising prices without checking churn.

Should a bubble-tea chain grow by franchising instead of opening its own shops?

Show the answer
  • Economics for us: fees and royalties against own-shop profits; capital needed.
  • Speed: shops opened per year each way; our capacity to manage growth.
  • Control: quality and brand consistency; choosing and supporting franchisees.
  • Economics for franchisees: their payback; whether good partners will sign up.

Where to start: economics for franchisees. If they cannot make money, the model fails.

The trap: looking only at our royalty income.
